paper_a.title: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities

metadata.description: Black-Scholes (1973) and Merton (1973) are the canonical parallel-rediscovery pair: contemporaneous derivations of the same European option pricing PDE and closed-form formula via different routes. Black-Scholes derive the PDE from a continuously rebalanced riskless hedge under CAPM-style equilibrium, while Merton derives a more general PDE (with stochastic bond price) from a no-arbitrage zero-net-investment portfolio that does NOT require CAPM. Merton additionally develops an extensive no-dominance/no-arbitrage bound theory (Theorems 1-13) that Black-Scholes do not cover, and treats dividends, perpetual American puts, down-and-out calls, and callable warrants. The shared core (PDE, closed-form formula, put-call parity, no-early-exercise of American calls) aligns tightly; Merton's broader theory is paper-specific.

matches.explanation: Both papers open with notation/definitions for call (warrant) and put options, American versus European exercise. Black-Scholes uses $w(x,t)$ for the call value; Merton uses $F, f, G, g$ for American/European warrant/put. The mathematical objects and roles are the same; only the symbol set differs.

Black-Scholes' option-value function $w(x,t)$ corresponds to Merton's $f(S,\tau;E)$ (European warrant) and $F(S,\tau;E)$ (American warrant). Same dependent variable up to time-to-expiry vs absolute time and inclusion of $E$ as an explicit argument.

Black-Scholes' single 'ideal market conditions' assumption block (constant $r$, log-normal $x$ with constant $v^2$, no dividends, frictionless trading, European exercise) is split in Merton across the global no-dominance Assumption 1 (more abstract/general, applies to the whole bound theory) and the explicit BSM-section SDEs for stock (geometric Brownian motion, EP370.3) and bond (EP370.4). Merton's setup is strictly more general because the bond is allowed to be stochastic, but the BSM specialization recovers Black-Scholes' assumptions.

Black-Scholes' explicit hedged-position construction (one share long, $1/w_1$ options short, equity $x - w/w_1$) is unique to their derivation. Merton replaces it with a zero-net-investment three-asset portfolio (stock, option, bond) with weights chosen to eliminate stochastic terms; he never names a 'hedge ratio' in this form.

Black-Scholes' 'variance rate $v^2$' (limit of the per-interval variance) is exactly Merton's $\sigma^2$ in the geometric Brownian motion SDE $dS/S = \alpha\,dt + \sigma\,dz$. Same parameter, different letter.

The notion of 'elasticity of option price with respect to stock price' ($xw_1/w$) is introduced in Black-Scholes specifically for their CAPM-based alternative derivation. Merton does not use elasticity language; his analogous quantity appears only implicitly via $H_1$ in Theorem 14.

Black-Scholes' Ito expansion $\Delta w = w_1\Delta x + \tfrac12 w_{11} v^2 x^2 \Delta t + w_2 \Delta t$ is the same Ito's-lemma application that Merton invokes in step 1 of his BSM PDE algorithm (ASP370.2.1) using $(dS)^2 = \sigma^2 S^2 dt$. Identical mathematical content.

The Black-Scholes PDE $w_2 = rw - rxw_1 - \tfrac12 v^2 x^2 w_{11}$ (TP369.1) is the special case of Merton's general parabolic PDE EP370.5 when $P(\tau) = e^{-r\tau}$ (deterministic bond, $\delta = 0$). Both reduce to the canonical Black-Scholes PDE in this limit. This is THE central shared result of the parallel rediscovery.

Both derive the PDE, but via fundamentally different portfolios. Black-Scholes (PP369.1) forms a riskless hedge of one share + $1/w_1$ short options and equates its certain return to $r\Delta t$; Merton (AP370.2) forms a zero-net-investment three-asset portfolio in stock + option + bond and chooses weights to zero $dz$ and $dq$ exposures, then imposes zero expected return. Same destination, different no-arbitrage machinery — Merton explicitly notes (RP370.2) that CAPM is sufficient but not necessary.

Composite L2 alignment of the two PDE-derivation step sequences. Both follow the same skeleton: (1) set up the hedging/replicating portfolio; (2) apply Ito to the option value; (3) impose no-arbitrage to eliminate stochastic terms; (4) rearrange to the parabolic PDE. The portfolios and arithmetic differ but the four-step pattern is shared.

Identical closed-form European call formula: Black-Scholes' $w(x,t) = xN(d_1) - c e^{r(t-t^*)} N(d_2)$ with $d_1, d_2$ as in eq. (13), and Merton's EP370.6 $f(S,\tau;E) = S\Phi(d_1) - E e^{-r\tau}\Phi(d_2)$. Same formula, the only difference is $\tau = t^*-t$ versus absolute $t$. Notably Merton's EP370.6 carries `origin: external` citing Black & Scholes 1973 — exactly the prior-work signature of parallel rediscovery.

Same solution technique: reduce the BS PDE to the heat equation by an explicit change of variables, apply the Gaussian-kernel solution, back-substitute. Black-Scholes cites Churchill (1963); Merton uses $h = H/(EP)$ with $x = S/(EP(\tau))$ and $T = \int_0^\tau V^2(s)\,ds$ to reach $\phi_2 = \tfrac12\phi_{11}$ then inverts. Merton's substitution is more general (handles time-varying volatility) but specializes to Black-Scholes' for constant $\sigma$.

Composite L2 alignment: both step sequences (i) substitute to reduce to heat equation, (ii) translate the boundary, (iii) apply Gaussian kernel, (iv) back-substitute. Black-Scholes spells this out as four PSP steps; Merton compresses it into two algorithm-steps but the substantive content matches.

Black-Scholes' explicit identity $w_1 = N(d_1)$ (the hedge-ratio-as-delta formula and the resulting elasticity bound $xw_1/w > 1$) does not appear as a named result in Merton. Merton's Theorem 14 proof uses $H_1$ but not in this packaged form.

Black-Scholes' 'alternative derivation' explicitly invokes the Capital Asset Pricing Model (Treynor, Sharpe, Lintner, Mossin) as an external cited theorem. Merton deliberately avoids CAPM (RP370.2: 'CAPM is a sufficient but not necessary assumption'); his framework predates the no-arbitrage cleanup that distinguishes the two papers.

The CAPM-based alternative derivation (cancellation of $a$ and $\beta_x$ terms) is unique to Black-Scholes. Merton's 'alternative' is simply the more rigorous no-arbitrage portfolio derivation, not a CAPM rederivation.
L2 step block of the CAPM alternative derivation has no Merton counterpart; included here only as a parent-skipped composite for completeness of the L1 PP369.3 'none' match.

Both state the no-early-exercise theorem for an American call on a non-dividend stock: such an option is never optimally exercised before maturity, so its value equals the European call value. Black-Scholes' CP369.1 explicitly attributes this to Merton (1973), confirming the alignment to TP370.2.

Put-call parity: Black-Scholes' $w - u = x - c e^{r(t-t^*)}$ and resulting put formula $u = -xN(-d_1) + c e^{r(t-t^*)} N(-d_2)$ correspond exactly to Merton's $g = f - S + E P(\tau)$ (TP370.12). Black-Scholes attribute this to Stoll (1969); Merton gives the full no-dominance proof in PP370.12.

Both papers explicitly remark that the option pricing formula does not depend on the expected return on the stock — a key conceptual insight of the no-arbitrage approach. RP369.1: 'eq. (13) does not contain the expected return'; RP370.1: 'price (21) does not depend on $\alpha$ ... or on risk preferences.' Identical observation.

Black-Scholes' specific remark that $t^*-t$ enters only as $r(t^*-t)$ and $v^2(t^*-t)$ (so an increase in maturity equals an equal percentage increase in $r$ and $v^2$) is an observation specific to the closed-form. Merton has Theorems 14 and 15 establishing monotonicity in $r$ and $\sigma^2$ separately but not this combined-parameter remark.

Both papers state the same root problem: determine the no-arbitrage value of a European call (warrant) with strike $E$ and maturity $\tau$ on a stock with given dynamics. Merton's framing is more general (no-dominance and constraint-derivation across the whole structural theory) but specializes to Black-Scholes' problem under BSM assumptions.

Black-Scholes' warrant valuation problem (long maturity, stepwise exercise prices, dividends, dilution) is treated by Merton via the dividend-adjusted PDE EP370.8 and the dynamic-programming algorithm AP370.1 for exercise-price schedules. Merton solves the parts of the problem that Black-Scholes only state.

Black-Scholes' application of the option formula to corporate stock and bond valuation (equity as a call on the firm's assets, compound option for coupon bonds) corresponds to Merton's OpenP370.2 — Section 11's program for treating corporate liabilities and term structure as contingent claims (the 'Cootner-Merton lines'). Black-Scholes carry this out in a focused way; Merton flags it as an open program.
Black-Scholes' empirical-test discussion (referencing Black & Scholes 1972) is paper-specific. Merton is a pure-theory paper with no empirical section.

Both papers flag the absence of a closed-form American put price as an open problem. Merton goes further than Black-Scholes by writing the obstacle-PDE EP370.9 explicitly and solving the perpetual case (EP370.10), but his OpenP370.1 'no closed-form American put for finite $\tau$' matches Black-Scholes' OpenP369.1 verbatim in spirit.

Black-Scholes flag the inadequacy of any exercise-price adjustment to protect against dividends (OpenP369.2). Merton resolves the protection question with a precise definition of payout-protection (DP370.4) and Theorem 11 + corollary giving the exact exercise-price adjustment ($\lambda = 1 + d/S_x$, exchange one warrant for $\lambda$ at $E/\lambda$) that achieves it. So Merton answers the question Black-Scholes posed as open — though Black-Scholes' edge case (holding company paying out all assets) is not captured by Merton's adjustment either.

Merton's Theorem 1 (lower bound $f \geq \max[0, S - EP(\tau)]$ on the European warrant) is the foundational no-dominance bound that drives Theorems 2, 3 and the put-call parity. Black-Scholes have no analog: they go straight to the PDE under their stronger BSM assumptions and never establish this distribution-free bound.
Merton's 'perpetual warrant equals the stock' theorem is unique to his bound theory; Black-Scholes only treat finite-maturity options.
Convexity of $F$ in exercise price $E$ has no Black-Scholes counterpart.
The Lipschitz bound $-P(\tau) \leq \partial f/\partial E \leq 0$ is unique to Merton's structural theory.
Scale homogeneity ($F_Q(kS, \tau; kE) = k F(S, \tau; E)$) is a Merton-only result derived from no-dominance.

Theorem 7 (warrant on a portfolio is bounded above by a portfolio of warrants) and its corollary (diversification hurts warrants) are unique Merton contributions, derived from convexity + no-dominance.

'Warrant price increases with riskiness' (Rothschild-Stiglitz mean-preserving spread monotonicity) is a Merton-only theorem; Black-Scholes only get monotonicity in $v^2$ as an immediate consequence of the closed-form (and even that is attributed to Merton's RP369.3).
Homogeneity-of-degree-1 in $(S, E)$ and convexity in $S$ under the D.I.S.P. condition are unique to Merton's structural theory.

Theorem 11 (payout-protection via the $\lambda = 1 + d/S_x$ adjustment) — already partially covered by the OpenP369.2 alignment above as 'analogous answer to an open question', but the theorem statement itself has no Black-Scholes counterpart.

Theorem 13 (American put strictly exceeds European put when there is positive probability of $f < E[1-P(T)]$) is uniquely Merton's; Black-Scholes' OpenP369.1 only acknowledges the inequality without the precise sufficient condition.

Comparative-statics theorems (warrant non-decreasing in interest rate, non-decreasing in $\sigma^2$). Black-Scholes mention these properties via Merton's RP369.3 (cited externally), but they do not state and prove them in their own paper.

Merton's appendix propositions (variance is a valid risk measure under BSM; counterexample showing D.I.S.P. is necessary for Theorems 9 and 10) are appendix-only structural results with no Black-Scholes analog.

Merton's terminal payoff $\max[0, S-E]$ and intrinsic-value lower bound are stated as named equations; Black-Scholes use the same boundary condition (eq. 8) but bundle it inside TP369.1 rather than as standalone results, so the 'objects' do not have a clean L1 partner.
Merton's continuous-dividend sufficient condition $E > d/r$ for no premature exercise is unique to his Section 3 dividend treatment.
Merton's dividend-adjusted PDE and the proportional/constant/continuously-changing dividend examples are Section 7 contributions absent from Black-Scholes (who explicitly assume no dividends).

American put PDE, perpetual American put closed form ($G = E/(1+\gamma)\,[(1+\gamma)S/(\gamma E)]^{-\gamma}$), and the free-boundary problem are uniquely Merton's. Black-Scholes only acknowledge the open problem (OpenP369.1).
Down-and-out call (Section 9) — barrier option pricing — is entirely a Merton extension; Black-Scholes do not consider barrier options.
Callable warrant valuation (Section 10) — the issuer's two-sided free-boundary problem with call price $K$ — is uniquely Merton's.

Merton's structural-theory primitives — Assumption 2 (distribution-only identification), the dominance and riskiness definitions, and the discount-bond price $P(\tau)$ — are foundational to his Section 2 bound theory but do not appear in Black-Scholes.

Merton's remark that the discrete-time Samuelson recursion is the correct formulation when dividends and exercise-price changes occur on discrete dates (with the continuous PDE as the approximation) is a methodological observation absent from Black-Scholes.
